lessons.title: Introduction to Exception Handling
lessons.description: Understand exceptions, errors and Java's exception hierarchy.
lessons.content:
Exception handling is a mechanism for detecting and responding to exceptional conditions during program execution.

Java uses Throwable as the root of its exception and error hierarchy.

Two important subclasses are:
1. Exception — Conditions applications may be able to handle.
2. Error — Serious problems that applications generally should not attempt to recover from.

Examples of exceptions include ArithmeticException, NullPointerException, NumberFormatException and IOException.

An exception can interrupt normal program execution. Java searches the call stack for a compatible exception handler.

Exception handling improves application reliability by allowing programs to handle expected failures appropriately.

Real-world example: A banking application must respond safely when a user enters an invalid amount or when a database operation fails.

examples.title: Division by Zero
examples.explanation: Demonstrates an ArithmeticException caused by integer division by zero.

lessons.title: try, catch and finally Blocks
lessons.description: Handle exceptions using Java's exception-handling blocks.
lessons.content:
The try block contains code that might throw an exception.

A catch block handles exceptions compatible with its declared type.

Multiple catch blocks may handle different exception types. More specific exception types must appear before their broader parent types.

The finally block normally executes after try and catch, whether an exception occurs or not. It is commonly used for cleanup, although try-with-resources is preferred for AutoCloseable resources.

The finally block is not absolutely guaranteed to execute in situations such as abrupt JVM termination.

A catch block should not silently ignore failures. Handle the exception appropriately or propagate it when necessary.

examples.title: Safe Division
examples.explanation: Handles integer division by zero and executes a finally block.

lessons.title: Checked and Unchecked Exceptions
lessons.description: Understand compile-time exception checking and runtime exceptions.
lessons.content:
Java distinguishes between checked and unchecked exceptions.

Checked exceptions must generally be caught or declared using throws. Examples include IOException and SQLException.

Unchecked exceptions include RuntimeException and its subclasses, such as ArithmeticException, IllegalArgumentException and NullPointerException.

Errors are also unchecked.

Checked exceptions commonly represent conditions that callers are expected to consider handling.

Unchecked exceptions often indicate programming mistakes or invalid arguments, although they can also represent other runtime failures.

The compiler checks whether checked exceptions are handled or declared. It does not guarantee that an application will be free from runtime exceptions.

Avoid catching Exception or Throwable unnecessarily because broad handlers can hide important problems.

examples.title: Checked Exception Example
examples.explanation: Handles IOException while reading a text file.

lessons.title: throw, throws and Custom Exceptions
lessons.description: Learn how to throw exceptions and declare exception propagation.
lessons.content:
The throw keyword explicitly throws an exception object.

The throws clause declares exceptions that a method may propagate to its caller.

For example, throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid age") creates and throws an unchecked exception.

A method that can propagate a checked IOException may declare throws IOException.

Custom exceptions represent application-specific failures.

A custom checked exception can extend Exception. A custom unchecked exception can extend RuntimeException.

Custom exceptions should have meaningful names and useful messages.

Use exceptions for exceptional situations rather than ordinary control flow.

Real-world example: An online payment system may throw InsufficientBalanceException when a withdrawal exceeds the available balance.

examples.explanation: Creates and throws an application-specific checked exception.

lessons.title: Try-with-Resources and Exception Best Practices
lessons.description: Manage resources safely and debug exceptions effectively.
lessons.content:
Try-with-resources automatically closes resources that implement AutoCloseable.

It is especially useful for files, streams, database connections and other resources that require cleanup.

Java closes declared resources in reverse order after the try block completes.

If both the try body and resource closing throw exceptions, the closing exception may be recorded as a suppressed exception.

Exception-handling best practices:
1. Catch specific exceptions where possible.
2. Preserve the original cause when wrapping exceptions.
3. Provide meaningful error messages.
4. Avoid empty catch blocks.
5. Validate input before performing operations.
6. Use try-with-resources for supported resources.
7. Do not expose sensitive implementation details to end users.

A stack trace identifies the exception type and the sequence of method calls involved in the failure.

quizzes.question: Which class is the root of Java's exception and error hierarchy?
quizzes.explanation: Throwable is the superclass of Exception and Error.

quizzes.question: Which block contains code that might throw an exception?
quizzes.explanation: The try block encloses statements that may throw exceptions.

quizzes.question: Which exception is thrown when Java integer division uses zero as the divisor?
quizzes.explanation: Integer division by zero causes an ArithmeticException.

quizzes.question: Which of the following is a checked exception?
quizzes.explanation: IOException is checked and generally must be caught or declared.

quizzes.question: What does the throw keyword do?
quizzes.explanation: throw explicitly throws an exception object.

quizzes.question: What is the purpose of a throws clause?
options: To declare exceptions that a method may propagate
quizzes.explanation: The throws clause declares exception types that a method may propagate to callers.

quizzes.question: Which statement about finally is correct?
options: It runs only when an exception occurs
It runs only when no exception occurs
It normally runs after try/catch regardless of whether an exception occurs
quizzes.explanation: finally normally executes after try/catch, but execution is not guaranteed in cases such as abrupt JVM termination.

quizzes.question: Which class should a custom checked exception normally extend?
quizzes.explanation: A custom checked exception commonly extends Exception without extending RuntimeException.

quizzes.question: What is the main benefit of try-with-resources?
options: It automatically closes declared AutoCloseable resources
quizzes.explanation: Try-with-resources closes declared AutoCloseable resources automatically.

quizzes.question: Which statement about multiple catch blocks is correct?
options: A broader superclass catch must always appear first
A specific subclass catch should appear before its broader superclass catch
quizzes.explanation: A broader catch placed before a more specific catch can make the specific catch unreachable.

exercises.title: Handle Division by Zero
exercises.instructions: Create a Java program that reads two integers using Scanner and divides them. Catch ArithmeticException when the divisor is zero. Display a helpful message without exposing an unhandled stack trace.

exercises.title: Validate Student Age
exercises.description: Use throw to reject invalid input.
exercises.instructions: Write a method registerStudent(int age). Throw IllegalArgumentException if age is less than 0 or greater than 120. Call the method with valid and invalid ages and handle the exception appropriately.

exercises.title: Build a Custom Banking Exception
exercises.description: Create and use a custom checked exception.
exercises.instructions: Create InsufficientBalanceException extending Exception. Implement a BankAccount class with deposit and withdraw methods. Throw the custom exception when the withdrawal exceeds the balance. Reject non-positive transaction amounts.

exercises.title: Read a File with Try-with-Resources
exercises.description: Handle file errors and close resources safely.
exercises.instructions: Write a Java program using BufferedReader and try-with-resources to read a text file line by line. Catch IOException and display a meaningful error message. Test with both an existing file and a missing file.

exercises.title: Debug Exception Catch Order
exercises.instructions: Consider: try { int n = Integer.parseInt("abc"); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("General"); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { System.out.println("Invalid number"); }. Explain why this does not compile. Rewrite the catch blocks in the correct order and test the program.
